questions.question: Which description defines an Euler tour of an undirected network?
options: A closed route that visits every vertex exactly once.
A closed route that uses every single edge exactly once.
A route that uses every edge exactly once, ending anywhere.
A closed route that uses every edge at least once.

questions.question: An Euler tour of an undirected network is a closed route that uses every edge exactly once. Vertex $A$ has four incident edges. May an Euler tour pass through $A$ more than once?
options: Yes; only edges are limited to one use each.
No; each vertex may be visited only once.
Only if $A$ is the start and end vertex.
Only if the edges at $A$ are parallel edges.

questions.question: An Euler tour of an undirected network is a closed route that uses every edge exactly once. Why must every vertex of a network with an Euler tour have even degree?
options: Because the start vertex has odd degree and all others are even.
Because every vertex must have at least two incident edges.
Because the total number of edges must be even.
Arrivals and departures at a vertex use its edges in pairs.

questions.question: In a weighted undirected network with an Euler tour (a closed route using every edge exactly once), how do the lengths of different Euler tours compare?
options: They depend on the order in which edges are used.
They depend on the starting vertex chosen.
All equal the sum of all the edge lengths.
The shortest one uses the shortest edges only.

questions.question: An undirected network has edges $A\text{-}B$, $B\text{-}C$, $C\text{-}D$, $D\text{-}A$, $A\text{-}C$, $C\text{-}E$ and $E\text{-}A$. An Euler tour of an undirected network is a closed route that uses every edge exactly once. Which vertex sequence is an Euler tour?
options: $A\text{-}B\text{-}C\text{-}D\text{-}A\text{-}E\text{-}A$
$A\text{-}B\text{-}C\text{-}A\text{-}D\text{-}C\text{-}E$
$A\text{-}B\text{-}C\text{-}D\text{-}A\text{-}C\text{-}E\text{-}A$
$A\text{-}B\text{-}C\text{-}D\text{-}A\text{-}C\text{-}A\text{-}E\text{-}A$

questions.question: An undirected network has two vertices $A$ and $B$ joined by two parallel edges $e_1$ and $e_2$, and no other edges. An Euler tour of an undirected network is a closed route that uses every edge exactly once. Does this network have an Euler tour?
options: No: going from $A$ to $B$ and back repeats an edge.
No: an Euler tour needs at least three vertices.
No: $A$ and $B$ have odd degree 1 each.
Yes: $A$ to $B$ along $e_1$, back along $e_2$.

questions.question: An undirected network has the triangle edges $A\text{-}B$, $B\text{-}C$, $C\text{-}A$ and a fourth vertex $D$ that lies on no edge. An Euler tour of an undirected network is a closed route that uses every edge exactly once. Does the network have an Euler tour?
options: No, since the tour never reaches vertex $D$.
No, since $D$ has degree 0, which is odd.
Yes: the route $A\text{-}B\text{-}C\text{-}A$.
Yes, but only after an edge to $D$ is added.

questions.question: In the course, a cycle is a path (distinct edges, vertices may repeat) that starts and ends at the same vertex. An Euler tour of an undirected network is a closed route that uses every edge exactly once. How are Euler tours and cycles related?
options: An Euler tour is never a cycle, as it may repeat vertices.
An Euler tour is a cycle only if no vertex repeats.
Every cycle that visits all vertices is an Euler tour.
It is a cycle that contains every edge of the network.

questions.question: An Euler tour of an undirected network is a closed route that uses every edge exactly once. A network has an Euler tour starting and ending at $A$. Can an Euler tour also start and end at another vertex $B$ that has incident edges?
options: Only if $B$ has the same degree as $A$.
No; the starting vertex of an Euler tour is fixed.
Yes; the closed tour can simply be started at $B$.
Only if $B$ has degree 2.

questions.question: An Euler tour of an undirected network is a closed route that uses every edge exactly once. A network has an Euler tour. One new edge is added between two different existing vertices $u$ and $v$. Can the enlarged network have an Euler tour?
options: Yes; the old tour plus the new edge forms a tour.
Yes, if the new edge is parallel to an existing one.
Yes, if the new edge is shorter than the others.
No; the degrees of $u$ and $v$ have now become odd.

questions.question: In an undirected network, the vertex sequence $A\text{-}B\text{-}C\text{-}A\text{-}D\text{-}C\text{-}E\text{-}A$ is an Euler tour (a closed route using every edge exactly once). What is the degree of $A$?
An Euler tour of an undirected network is a closed route that uses every edge exactly once. Which network, given by its edges, has an Euler tour?
options: $A\text{-}B$, $B\text{-}C$, $C\text{-}A$, $A\text{-}D$, $D\text{-}E$, $E\text{-}A$
$A\text{-}B$, $A\text{-}C$, $A\text{-}D$, $B\text{-}C$, $B\text{-}D$, $C\text{-}D$
$A\text{-}B$, $B\text{-}C$, $C\text{-}D$, $D\text{-}A$, $A\text{-}C$
$A\text{-}B$, $A\text{-}C$, $A\text{-}D$, $A\text{-}E$

questions.question: A connected undirected network has 9 edges and an Euler tour (a closed route using every edge exactly once). The tour is written as a vertex sequence whose first and last entries are the starting vertex. How many entries does the sequence have?

An Euler tour of an undirected network is a closed route that uses every edge exactly once. In a network with an Euler tour, the edge $u\text{-}v$ is removed. Can $u$ and $v$ then be left without any path between them?
options: No; the rest of the tour still leads from $v$ back to $u$.
Yes, if $u\text{-}v$ was the only edge between those two vertices.
Yes, if $u$ or $v$ has degree 2.
Only if the network has parallel edges can they stay joined.

questions.question: An Euler tour of an undirected network is a closed route that uses every edge exactly once. Every vertex of an undirected network has even degree, but the edges form two triangles with no vertex in common. Does the network have an Euler tour?
options: Yes, since every vertex has even degree.
No; a closed route cannot get from one triangle to the other.
Yes, by touring one triangle and then the other.
No, since one triangle's vertices then have odd degree.

questions.question: A network has edges $A\text{-}B$, $B\text{-}C$, $C\text{-}D$, $D\text{-}A$, $A\text{-}E$ and $E\text{-}B$. An Euler tour of an undirected network is a closed route that uses every edge exactly once. Exactly one edge is to be removed so that an Euler tour can exist. Which edge?
options: $A\text{-}B$
$A\text{-}E$
$C\text{-}D$
$E\text{-}B$

questions.question: A network has edges $P\text{-}Q$, $Q\text{-}R$, $R\text{-}S$, $S\text{-}P$, $P\text{-}R$, $R\text{-}T$ and $T\text{-}S$. A snowplough starts at $P$ and clears every edge exactly once, not necessarily returning. At which vertex must it finish?
options: At $P$
At $R$
At $S$
At $T$
